advances: Finite scalar concave sequences, including zero endpoints. The result concerns adjacent power moments and their sharp homogeneous ratio.

proof:
Concavity means that successive differences are nonincreasing. First consider any concave arm $r_0=1,r_1,\ldots,r_h$ with $0\le r_i\le1$. If $h=0$, its contribution to $\sum_i(r_i^2-2r_i/3)$ is $1/3$. For $h\ge1$, use the equal-square affine replacement $g_i=1+\eta i$ of accepted fact 4d628efe7673ce2d (5). Its hypotheses hold because the arm is nonnegative and anchored at one. The square sum is strictly increasing over the admissible slopes, and $\sum_{i=1}^h r_i^2\le h$, so $\eta\le0$. By the fixed-length proof of (5), the differences $r_i^2-g_i^2$ have a nonnegative prefix and a nonpositive suffix. They sum to zero. On their nonzero indices $r_i+g_i>0$, and these denominators are nonincreasing since both arms are nonincreasing. If there are nonzero differences, take the denominator at the last positive difference. Dividing the positive differences by their own denominators gives at most division by this common number, and so does dividing the negative differences by their own, smaller denominators. Therefore $\sum_i(r_i-g_i)\le0$, also when all square differences vanish. It follows that the replacement does not increase the quadratic objective.

For an affine arm of slope $\eta$, the objective is
$$
\frac{h+1}{3}+\frac43\eta\sum_{i=0}^h i+\eta^2\sum_{i=0}^h i^2.
$$
For $h\ge1$ the minimum occurs at $\eta=-2/(2h+1)$, an admissible slope since the endpoint is $1/(2h+1)$. The minimum is $(h+1)/(3(2h+1))$, also valid for $h=0$. Given a nonnegative concave sequence $g$ of length $n$ and peak $b>0$ at $j$, apply this result to the normalized left and right arms oriented away from $j$. Subtract the duplicate peak term $1/3$ and rescale. This gives
$$
\sum_i g_i^2-\frac23 b\sum_i g_i
\ge \frac{b^2}{6}\left(\frac1{2j+1}+\frac1{2(n-1-j)+1}\right)
\ge\frac{b^2}{3n},
$$
where the last inequality uses $u^{-1}+v^{-1}\ge4/(u+v)$ for positive $u,v$ and $u+v=2n$. The last bound at $g=f$ proves the statement for $p=1$.

For $p>1$, divide $f$ by $m$ so that the maximum is one, and put $g_i(t)=(f_i-t)_+$ for $0\le t<1$, using $s_+=\max\{s,0\}$. The indices with $f_i>t$ are consecutive by concavity, and on that block $g_i(t)=f_i-t$ is concave with maximum $1-t$. Apply the quadratic bound to that block, whose length is at most $N$. Insert the zeros outside the block in the sums after applying the bound to obtain
$$
3\sum_i g_i(t)^2-2(1-t)\sum_i g_i(t)\ge (1-t)^2/N.
$$
This also holds with both sides zero at $t=1$. Multiply by $t^{p-2}$ and integrate over $0<t<1$. The sum is finite, and the factors other than $t^{p-2}$ are bounded, so the integrations exist even for $1<p<2$. For any $x\in[0,1]$, expansion of the powers gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^x t^{p-2}(x-t)^2\,dt
 &=\frac{2x^{p+1}}{(p-1)p(p+1)},\\
\int_0^x t^{p-2}(1-t)(x-t)\,dt
 &=\frac{x^p}{(p-1)p}-\frac{x^{p+1}}{p(p+1)}.
\end{aligned}
$$
These formulas also hold at $x=0$. Substitution into the integrated inequality gives the desired estimate after cancelling $2/((p-1)p(p+1))$. Homogeneity restores the factor $m^{p+1}$. The positive correction gives the strict ratio inequality, and for $N=1$ the finite inequality is an equality.

For sharpness at fixed $p$, take $f_i=1-|i|/h$ for $-h\le i\le h$ with integers $h\to\infty$. These are nonnegative concave sequences of maximum one. For $q=p,p+1$, the Riemann sums $h^{-1}\sum_i f_i^q$ converge to $2/(q+1)$, by integration on $[-1,1]$. Their ratio tends to $(p+1)/(p+2)$.
statement:
Let $f_0,\ldots,f_{N-1}$ be a nonnegative, nonzero concave sequence on consecutive indices, with $N\ge1$ and $m=\max_i f_i$. For every real $p\ge1$,
$$
(p+2)\sum_i f_i^{p+1}-(p+1)m\sum_i f_i^p\ge\frac{m^{p+1}}{N}.
$$
Consequently $\sum_i f_i^{p+1}/(m\sum_i f_i^p)>(p+1)/(p+2)$ for every finite sequence. At each fixed $p$, the latter constant is the infimum over all finite lengths and all such sequences.
title: Finite real-power moment inequality for concave sequences
